From January 2026, borrowers of power tools would pay a refundable deposit of GBP 10, which the service expects to reduce damage and late returns. Members receiving Council Tax Reduction would continue to borrow free of charge.
  para 12 The committee is asked to approve the continuation and extension of the Library of Things as set out above, funded from the libraries budget and from loan fees.

```
# Kestle Bay heat pump programme: board meeting notes, 14 November 2024

## Kestle Bay heat pump programme: board meeting notes, 14 November 2024

Present: Rosa Penhallow (chair), Daniel Kitto, Meera Joshi, Tom Rowe and Ellen Vosper (programme manager). Apologies: Gareth Lobb.

## Progress

Ellen reported that the first phase closed in September with 214 installations. Installers now report a median of 9 weeks between the home survey and the installation date, down from 14 weeks in the first year of the programme.

## Installers

Brightwater Heating withdrew from the programme in August because of staff shortages, leaving Pellow and Sons as the only appointed installer. The board agreed to run a new tender in January to appoint at least one more installer before phase two begins.

## Complaints

Six formal complaints were received in 2024, four of them about installation delays and two about the condition of gardens after outdoor units were fitted. All have been resolved.

## Phase two

The board agreed a target of 150 further installations by March 2026, with priority for homes heated by oil or bottled gas. It also agreed to cap the householder contribution at GBP 4,000 for households receiving means-tested benefits, with the society's hardship fund meeting the rest of the cost.

## Actions

Ellen to draft the installer tender by 12 December. Daniel to ask the Coastal Communities Net Zero Fund whether the grant can stay at GBP 6,000 per home in phase two. Meera to update the website with the new waiting times.
```

rows.text:
s1 = Reviews/Library of Things pilot evaluation.pdf @f920bb864b23
[1] s1 text:
  p.1 Borrowing instead of buying: evaluation of the Brackenford Library of Things pilot, April 2023 to March 2025
  p.1 Northfold Social Research, for Brackenford Libraries. Final report, September 2025.
  p.1 The Brackenford Library of Things lends household tools and equipment from three branch libraries for a small fee. This report evaluates the first two years of the pilot, from April 2023 to March 2025, using membership and loan records, a survey of borrowers and the checks that staff make when items are returned. Almost 2,000 residents registered as borrowers, and loans grew by 64 percent between the first and second years. Borrowers reported modest savings, and most items came back in good condition. Registrations from deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with their share of the town's population. We recommend that the scheme continues, with changes to how damage is recorded and how new items are chosen.
  p.1 Libraries of things apply the familiar library model to objects that households need only occasionally, such as drills, gazebos and sewing machines. Their supporters argue that borrowing saves money, reduces the number of rarely used items that people buy, and brings people into libraries who would not otherwise visit.
  p.1 Brackenford Libraries opened its Library of Things in April 2023 with a grant of GBP 96,000 from the Halden Foundation, which also funded this evaluation. The pilot ran from three of the town's seven branch libraries: Central, Eastgate and Millbrook.
  p.2 Items could be reserved online and collected from any of the three branches, and loans lasted up to seven days. This report sets out what the pilot achieved against the aims agreed with the funder: to reach a broad range of residents, to build regular use, to save households money and to reduce waste. Section 2 summarises earlier evaluations of similar schemes, Section 3 describes our methods, Section 4 presents the results, and Sections 5 to 7 discuss them.
  p.2 Published evaluations of libraries of things are few, and most describe a single scheme in its first years. A survey of 14 schemes in England found a median of 1,150 registered borrowers per scheme after two years of operation, with wide variation by town size (Carraway Trust, 2022). The same survey reported a median household saving of GBP 60 a year among borrowers who answered its questionnaire.
  p.2 Repeat borrowing, the share of borrowers who borrow more than once, is often used as a sign that a scheme has become part of household routines. It was 34 percent at the Harwick Tool Library in its second year (Pemberton and Shah, 2021) and 39 percent at the Otterburn Share Shed (Lindqvist, 2023). Damage rates reported by tool libraries usually fall between 2 and 5 percent of loans, with power tools at the upper end of that range (Odum, 2020).
  p.2 Estimates of environmental benefit vary more widely. Faraday and Mbeki (2022) estimated that a large urban scheme avoided 52 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in a year, but noted that the result depended heavily on what borrowers said they would otherwise have bought. No published study that we are aware of has followed a scheme in a town of Brackenford's size for more than one year.
  p.3 At launch the catalogue held 164 items, chosen by library staff after a public consultation, and by March 2025 it had grown to 236 items. Standard members paid between GBP 1 and GBP 6 per loan, depending on the item, while members receiving Council Tax Reduction borrowed free of charge. Staff checked each item on return against a written checklist and recorded any damage on the loan record.
  p.3 3.2 Membership and loan records
  p.3 We analysed the anonymised membership and loan records for the whole pilot period. Each loan record held the item, the branch, the dates of issue and return, the fee paid and any damage recorded at return. Membership records held the branch of registration and the home postcode, which we used to assign each borrower to a deprivation quintile of the Index of Multiple Deprivation.
  p.3 In February 2025 we sent an online survey to all 1,421 members who had borrowed at least one item, and paper copies were offered at all three branches. The survey asked what borrowers had used items for, what they would have done without the scheme, and how much they thought they had saved. It received 426 responses, a response rate of 30 percent.
  p.3 3.4 Avoided purchases and emissions
  p.3 We estimated avoided purchases by applying the share of survey respondents who said they would otherwise have bought each type of item to the number of different members who borrowed that type of item, so that repeat loans of the same item by the same member were counted once. Emissions were then estimated from the weight and main material of each type of item, using published factors for the manufacture of household equipment (Faraday and Mbeki, 2022).
  p.4 We report counts and percentages for the whole pilot and for each year, where year one runs from April 2023 to March 2024 and year two from April 2024 to March 2025. Before analysis we removed 203 loan records that staff had created to test the booking system or that had been recorded twice because of a software fault in the summer of 2023.
  p.4 By the end of March 2025, 1,936 people had registered as borrowers across the three branches. Just over half registered at Central, which is the largest branch and the only one open on Sundays (Table 1).
  p.4 Table 1. Registered borrowers by branch of registration, April 2023 to March 2025
  p.4 Of the 1,490 borrowers with a usable home postcode, 611 (41 percent) lived in neighbourhoods in the two most deprived quintiles. This is close to the 40 percent of Brackenford residents who live in those neighbourhoods. The remaining 446 registrations had no usable postcode, mostly because borrowers had registered with a work address, and they are not included in this figure.
  p.5 4.2 Loans and repeat use

[title Warmer homes, lower bills? Evaluation of the Kestle Bay Community Heat Pump Programme, 2022 to 2024]
